title: 2021 Fall AMC 12A Problem 17
statement: For how many ordered pairs \((b, c)\) of positive integers does neither \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\) nor \(x^2 + cx + b = 0\) have two distinct real solutions?

solutions.text:
Neither quadratic has two distinct real roots exactly when both discriminants are nonpositive: \(b^2 \le 4c\) and \(c^2 \le 4b.\)

Combining \(c\ge \frac{b^2}{4}\) with \(c\le2\sqrt b\) gives \(b^{\frac{3}{2}}\le8,\) so \(b\le4.\) Checking: \(b = 1\) gives \(c \in \{1,2\};\) \(b = 2\) gives \(c \in \{1,2\};\) \(b = 3\) gives \(c = 3;\) and \(b = 4\) gives \(c = 4.\)

That is \((1,1),\) \((1,2),\) \((2,1),\) \((2,2),\) \((3,3),\) \((4,4)\) — \(6\) ordered pairs.

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: “No two distinct real solutions” means each discriminant is \(\le 0:\) \(b^2 \le 4c\) and \(c^2 \le 4b\)
Multiplying gives \(b^2c^2 \le 16bc,\) so \(bc \le 16;\) test small positive integers
